newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia to loosen interest withholding tax.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia to loosen interest withholding tax.

text.p: The Australian parliament is expected to pass in the next few months a bill to loosen interest withholding tax to keep up with current financial market practise, government officials said on Friday.
The bill, foreshadowed by the government last year, would also try to restrict avoidance of the 10 percent tax, which is generally payable on interest that Australians pay to foreigners.
There is an exemption to the tax and the new Taxation Laws Amendment Bill (No.2) 1997 would widen that exemption.
"The aim is to modernise the exemption, to bring it into like with current financing practice," a spokesman for the Tax Office told Reuters.
As the law stands, the tax is not payable if the borrowings meet certain requirements, including that they are used for business purposes and raised by a widely placed issue of debentures.

The new system would abolish the business-use requirement, effectively making foreign money available for consumer loans, and require only a public offering in the wholesale market instead of wide retail placement.
The public offer could be made electronically, through Reuters for example, the government said in an explanation of its bill circulated to members of parliament.
The exemption is available only to financing between unrelated companies and will remain so after the amendment.
The bill includes some procedural changes and a crackdown on avoidance.
Australia has a set of general rules against tax avoidance but they do not currently apply to withholding tax.
The bill would extend those general rules to withholding tax and also prevent some particular avoidance techniques that the government has identified.
For example, it would impose the tax on income streams that are not technically interest but are similar to interest.

The new measures would also "ensure that withholding tax is payable where tax-exempt bodies are interposed between an Australian resident payer and a non-resident recipient," the governnment told parliament.
And the bill would remove doubt that the tax applied to dividends paid from capital reserves.
The government normally aims to have a bill pass through both houses of parliament in a single session.
The current session ends in March.
The changes to the tax were initiated by the former Labor government.
